name: Canyon
notes: Pinyon-juniper and scrub on rocky rims and slopes, cottonwood and willow galleries along the canyon floor stream, ferns at seeps; Colorado Plateau canyons (Grand Canyon, Zion) with Copper Canyon and Fish River Canyon analogues.

canopy.silhouette: broad open crown on massive pale trunk, yellow autumn

growth.juvenile_note: Seeds germinate within 24-48 h on wet, bare sand left by receding spring floods, and the tiny seedling's root must keep pace with the falling water table (4-13 mm a day). Survivors form dense, even-aged bands of slender whips along the channel, with shiny, broadly triangular, coarsely toothed leaves on flattened stalks that turn gold in autumn.
growth.source: USDA FEIS Populus fremontii (germinates within 24-48 h; seed viable 1-5 weeks, lost if not in a wet microsite in 2-3 days; seedling roots grow 4-12 mm a day; reproductive at 5-10 yr; 6-34 m tall; lives more than 130 yr; wind pollinated). Height-growth years estimated from riparian cottonwood growth rates.

fruiting.source: USDA FEIS Populus fremontii (flowers early spring, done by end of May; male catkins 3.8-8.3 cm, female 10-12.7 cm; seed shed Feb-June by region; entirely wind pollinated). Capsule size, days to ripen and crop follow P. deltoides (USDA Silvics); colour is the red male catkins.

canopy.silhouette: multi-stem clonal oak thicket, rounded crowns

growth.juvenile_note: Hypogeal: the acorn stays in the soil, drives down a taproot and builds a woody lignotuber while the top is only 10-20 cm with a few deeply round-lobed leaves. Rhizomes then send up many slender stems, so young plants look like a clump of thin grey-barked sprouts (oak brush) thickening into a dense thicket; after fire, sprouts reach about 45 cm in the first summer.
growth.source: USDA FEIS Quercus gambelii (stems: typical death 90 yr, max 120, some 142; stands mature at 60-80 yr; sprouts 41-46 cm the first summer; clones spread ~10 cm/yr; shrub 0.9-6 m or tree to 23 m; few acorns from stems under 5 cm dbh); first acorn age and germination estimated

fruiting.source: USDA FEIS Quercus gambelii (flowers late Mar-Apr in Arizona, May-Jun in Utah when leaves are half grown; acorns take 4-6 months, mature Sep-early Oct, usually 1.9 x 1.6 cm; ~188,000 acorns/acre, over 331,000 in wet years; most from stems 30-36 cm dbh); per-stem crop and decay estimated

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal: two notched, rounded cotyledons, then small rough leathery ovate leaves with a lopsided base and a raised net of veins below. The seedling is a thin zig-zag whip that grows slowly; drought, browsing and resprouting often make it a crooked, several-stemmed small tree.
growth.source: USDA FEIS Celtis laevigata var. reticulata (grows slowly, usually 2-6 m, to 16 m; lives 100-200 yr; flowers Apr-May with the leaves; drupes orange-red to purple or black, sweet, persist through winter; abundant crops most years; 120-day cold stratification, 37-80% germination)

fruiting.source: USDA FEIS Celtis laevigata var. reticulata (inconspicuous flowers with the new leaves Apr-May; drupe ~6 mm stone, orange-red to purple, sweet pulp eaten by birds, mammals and people; ripens late summer-fall and persists into winter; heavy crops nearly every year)

growth.juvenile_note: Seedlings rise from seeds buried in jay caches, often under a juniper or shrub: epigeal, with 6-10 cotyledons and bluish primary needles, then stiff, curved, paired needles. Young trees are compact, bushy, rounded cones with branches to the ground; old trees become broad, dome-crowned and often multi-trunked.
growth.source: USDA Silvics (Ronco): seedlings grow 2.5-5 cm/yr, saplings 10-15 cm/yr, mature trees 5-10 cm/yr; cones from ~25 yrs, seed in quantity at 75-100; good crops every 4-7 yrs; intolerant of shade; dominants often 400 yrs, some 800-1,000; jays and nutcrackers cache the seed

fruiting.source: USDA Silvics (flowers late May-June from buds formed the previous August; seeds mature early September of the second summer and cones open from mid-September over ~50 days; 10-20 large wingless seeds per cone); crop and decay estimated

growth.juvenile_note: Seedlings have needle-like juvenile leaves 5-10 mm long, making a soft, prickly little blue-green cone; scale leaves take over within a few years. Growth is very slow (often only a few cm a year) and seedlings usually establish under a nurse shrub, becoming after decades a rounded, bushy, often multi-trunked tree with shreddy grey bark.
growth.source: USDA Woody Plant Seed Manual (J. osteosperma: flowers Mar-Apr, cones ripen in 2nd year, reddish-brown with bloom, persist ~2 yr, 1-2 seeds, good crops about every 2 yr, bears from 10-20 yr); Wikipedia (3-6 m, cones 8-13 mm maturing in ~18 months, juvenile needles 5-10 mm). Growth rate and longevity estimated.

fruiting.source: Wikipedia (cones 8-13 mm, blue-brown with whitish waxy bloom, mature in ~18 months, pollen shed early spring; eaten and dispersed by jackrabbits, coyotes, solitaires); USDA WPSM (reddish-brown ripe cones persist ~2 yr). Set, crop and rot estimated.

shrub.silhouette: silver-grey rounded sage bush, shreddy trunk

growth.juvenile_note: Seedling: two small round cotyledons, then narrow, entire, silvery-hairy leaves; the wedge-shaped leaves with three blunt teeth at the tip come a few weeks later. It stays a single-stemmed silver sprig for a year or two while its roots race down, then branches into a rounded, aromatic, silver-grey bush with a short twisted trunk and shreddy bark.
growth.source: USDA FEIS Artemisia tridentata subsp. tridentata: germination in 2-3 days at all test temperatures, in late fall/winter or after snowmelt; plants 2-3 yr old can bear viable seed; commonly 40-50 yr, some over 100 yr; 1-2 m, up to 5 m. Height-age curve and shade class estimated.

fruiting.source: USDA FEIS basin big sagebrush: flowers late Aug-Oct; seed ripens and disperses Oct-Dec over ~8 weeks, ~90% within 9 m; self- or wind-pollinated; more prolific than Wyoming big sagebrush. Tiny heads of a few florets in leafy panicles; fruit set and crop estimated.

shrub.silhouette: dark spiny low mound, nearly black at distance

growth.juvenile_note: Seedlings usually come up in clumps from forgotten rodent seed caches: tiny epigeal seedlings with two oval cotyledons and small narrow opposite leaves; most die at the cotyledon stage. Survivors grow very slowly into a dense, rounded, rigidly branched grey shrub whose twigs end in spines and turn blackish when wet, hence the name.
growth.source: USDA FEIS Coleogyne ramosissima (slow-growing shrub 0.3-1.8 m on shallow soils, long-lived, flowers in spring from buds formed ~2 wk after March growth, apetalous solitary terminal flowers, wind-pollinated, achenes 3-4 mm, a masting species, rodent caches give clumped seedlings, 53-83% germination with 7 wk stratification, most seedlings die); ages estimated

fruiting.source: USDA FEIS Coleogyne ramosissima (solitary terminal flowers with 4 yellowish petal-like sepals and no petals, spring only; wind pollination; dry leathery achenes 3-4 mm with a twisted style, ripe early summer; mast years with huge crops, scatter-hoarded by rodents)

growth.juvenile_note: Seeds germinate in spring after winter chilling. The seedling puts most of its growth into roots at first (high root:shoot ratio), above ground showing only a few small, thick, dark green leaves cut into 3-5 narrow lobes with rolled-under edges and sticky gland dots. It grows slowly into a stiff, much-branched sprig with shreddy grey-red bark, often wedged in rock cracks.
growth.source: USDA FEIS Purshia stansburiana (needs overwinter or 1-2 months cold stratification; early growth mainly below ground; first seed at about age 5, good crops about every 2 yr; oldest sampled plant 69 yr, modal age 40-45 yr; usually 0.3-1.8 m, up to 7.6 m). Height-growth years estimated.

fruiting.source: USDA FEIS Purshia stansburiana (flowers early May to late June, some until frost; April-Sept in AZ and CA; persistent style 1-3.5 cm, several times longer than the achene); Wikipedia (fragrant cream-white flowers; feathery plume to 6 cm, spread by wind and rodents). Ripening, crop and decay estimated.

From the second year root suckers send up straight, unbranched wand-like stems around it, so a young plant is a spreading thicket of slim grey-green whips (clones up to 325 m2).

fruiting.source: USDA FEIS Salix exigua (catkins 1.5-10 cm with or just after the leaves, peak May, sporadic all summer; primarily insect pollinated; seed dispersal mid-May to mid-July, sometimes to October); fruit set and crop estimated

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal: two narrow needle-like cotyledons, then thin, bright green jointed stems with tiny scale leaves. Weak early growth: after 5-10 years it is a knee-high (60 cm) tuft of many parallel, upright, bright green twigs like a broom; later a dense rounded mound to 1.5 m that resprouts from the root crown after fire.
growth.source: USDA FEIS species review (Ephedra viridis): 4-week prechill, germination over ~28 days; weak seedlings reaching 0.6 m after 5-10 yr; grows best in full sun; dominant post-fire resprouter; Ephedra spp. live >100 yr.

fruiting.source: USDA FEIS (Ephedra viridis: dioecious, wind-pollinated in spring; nut-like seeds in bract cones mature Jul 15-Sep 1; abundant crops very infrequent; seeds dispersed and cached by small mammals). Colours, fruit set, hang, rot, crop estimated from the genus.

growth.source: Wikipedia Opuntia engelmannii (clumps to 3.5 m; pads 15-30 x 12-20 cm; flowers Apr-May lasting 1-2 days, yellow, 6-9 cm, bee pollinated; purple fruits 3.5-9 cm, edible); seedling growth and ages estimated from Opuntia demography studies

growth.juvenile_note: Seedlings emerge with the summer rains (June-July) as a thin tuft of narrow grey-green blades; roots reach about 25 cm in 6 weeks. From the second year scaly rhizomes 2.5-5 cm deep creep out (up to 1.5-1.8 m) and send up new tufts, so the plant becomes a patchy sod of stiff, curly-bladed culms 20-50 cm tall topped by compact spikes 3-7 cm long.
growth.source: USDA FEIS Pleuraphis jamesii (85% germination at 15.5-32 C; seedling roots 24.7 cm at 6 weeks; emergence June-July; rhizomes 1.5-1.8 m long, persist 5-7+ yr; resprouts regain preburn cover within 2 yr; culms 8-61 cm; spikes 3-7 cm). Age at first seed and plant lifespan estimated.
